core: Aggregate supply (AS) as the total real output (real GDP) that firms are willing to produce and sell at each aggregate price level
The short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve slopes upward because input prices are slow to adjust, so a higher output price level widens profit margins and induces more production
The long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve is vertical at potential (full-employment) GDP, where output is fixed by resources and technology rather than the price level
What shifts aggregate supply: input/resource prices (energy, wages) and productivity/technology
The AD-AS equilibrium, where aggregate demand crosses aggregate supply, jointly determines the equilibrium price level and equilibrium real GDP
Supply shocks and stagflation: a negative supply shock shifts SRAS left, raising the price level while cutting real output, illustrated by the 1973-74 oil shock
supporting: The macro AD-AS diagram plots the aggregate price level (GDP deflator) on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis, unlike a micro single-good supply-demand diagram
The AS curve is often drawn as a single curve that is nearly flat (Keynesian zone) below potential and nearly vertical (neoclassical zone) near potential GDP
Say's Law (supply creates its own demand) is a reasonable approximation for the long run, matching the vertical LRAS
outOfScope: Why the aggregate demand curve slopes downward and its components C+I+G+NX — owned by economics:foundations:aggregate-demand
The long-run rightward drift of potential output / LRAS over decades — owned by economics:foundations:economic-growth
Recession and expansion dating and the phases of fluctuation — owned by economics:foundations:business-cycle
The definition and measurement of GDP and of inflation/CPI — owned by economics:foundations:gdp and economics:foundations:inflation

claims.claim: The aggregate supply curve shows the total quantity of output (real GDP) that firms will produce and sell at each price level, and firms base output decisions on expected profit, set by output prices relative to input costs.

The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward because when the price level of final goods rises while input prices stay fixed, firms' profit margins improve, and the lure of higher profit induces them to expand production.

Potential GDP is the amount of real GDP an economy can produce by fully employing its existing levels of labor, physical capital, and technology; at that output the economy is at full employment and the AS curve becomes nearly vertical, so output near potential is limited by capacity rather than by the price level.

In the long run an economy faces genuine limits on output set by the quantity of labor, physical capital, technology, and institutional/market structures, so long-run output tracks productive capacity rather than the price level; Say's Law (supply creates its own demand) is a reasonable approximation for the long run.

A rise in the price of a widely used input such as labor or energy shifts the SRAS curve to the left, while falling input prices shift it to the right; a higher level of productivity shifts the AS curve to the right because firms can then produce more output at every price level.

A negative supply shock shifts aggregate supply left and produces stagflation: reduced GDP or recession, higher unemployment, and a higher (inflationary) price level at the same time; the U.S. experienced this in the 1970s following oil price surges.

In the 1973-74 oil shock, OAPEC imposed an oil embargo on the United States beginning October 19, 1973; production cuts nearly quadrupled the price of oil from $2.90 a barrel before the embargo to $11.65 a barrel by January 1974 (about a 4.0x increase, verified in Bash), and the embargo was lifted in March 1974 while the higher prices remained.

In the AD-AS model, equilibrium occurs where the aggregate demand and aggregate supply curves intersect, jointly determining the equilibrium price level and the equilibrium level of real GDP; the vertical axis is the aggregate price level (GDP deflator) and the horizontal axis is real GDP.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether aggregate supply should be drawn as one upward-sloping curve that becomes vertical at potential GDP, or as two separate curves (an upward SRAS and a vertical LRAS).
positions: OpenStax's Principles of Macroeconomics 3e draws a single AS curve that is nearly flat well below potential (Keynesian zone) and nearly vertical near potential GDP (neoclassical zone).
Many intermediate textbooks draw an explicitly separate short-run AS curve and a distinct vertical long-run AS curve at potential output.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the standard two-curve intuition (upward SRAS, vertical LRAS at potential GDP) because it makes the short-run vs long-run distinction explicit, and notes that a single steepening curve is the equivalent OpenStax presentation; the economics is the same.

sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: the AS curve as 'the total quantity of output (i.e. real GDP) that firms will produce and sell at each price level'; firms deciding output on expected profit (output prices vs input costs); SRAS sloping up because a higher final-goods price level with fixed input prices improves margins and the 'lure of higher profits' induces more output; potential GDP as 'the amount of real GDP an economy can produce by fully employing its existing levels of labor, physical capital, and technology' (full-employment GDP); the curve steepening from the flat Keynesian zone toward the vertical neoclassical zone near potential; equilibrium where AD and AS intersect setting the equilibrium price level and real GDP; vertical axis = price level (GDP deflator), horizontal axis = real GDP. REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.

sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)

REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, Section 11.1: Macroeconomic Perspectives on Demand and Supply
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: Say's Law ('supply creates its own demand') as 'a good approximation for the long run' where productive-capacity growth drives demand growth; Keynes' Law ('demand creates its own supply') applying better 'in the short run of a few months to a few years'; and that economies face 'genuine limits to how much they can produce, limits determined by the quantity of labor, physical capital, technology, and the institutional and market structures' — the basis for a long-run output level set by capacity rather than the price level.
